title: Horizon-Specific Machine Learning Forecasting of Hourly Ozone Concentrations Using an Automated EPA AirData Pipeline
content: Accurate short-term ozone forecasting is essential for protecting public health, supporting environmental management, and improving operational air-quality monitoring systems. However, many existing studies evaluate only a limited number of forecasting models, rely on a single train–test partition, and provide little evidence regarding model robustness, 5 statistical significance, or feature interpretability. To address these limitations, this study proposes a fully automated and reproducible machine-learning framework for horizon-specific hourly ozone forecasting using long-term observations from the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) AirData network. The proposed workflow integrates automated station selection, temporal quality assessment, missing-value reconstruction, advanced feature engineering, benchmarking of multiple regression algorithms, chronological hold-out evaluation, expanding- and rolling-window temporal cross-validation, non-parametric statistical testing, explainability analysis, feature selection, and systematic feature-family ablation. The experimental results demonstrate that forecasting performance is strongly horizon-dependent. XGBoost achieved the highest predictive accuracy for the 1-hour forecasting horizon (RMSE = 0.004643, R2 = 0.9248), ExtraTrees performed best for the 6-hour horizon (RMSE = 0.008877, R2 = 0.7255), XGBoost again ranked first at 12 hours (RMSE = 0.009753, R2 = 0.6690), whereas Gradient Boosting provided the best performance for the 24-hour horizon (RMSE = 0.009933, R2 = 0.6571). Temporal validation confirmed the robustness of these results, while statistical tests demonstrated significant differences among competing models. Explainability and ablation analyses further revealed that cyclical temporal descriptors, rolling ozone statistics, and autoregressive variables contributed most strongly to predictive performance. Overall, the proposed framework provides a robust, interpretable, and fully reproducible methodology for horizon-specific ozone forecasting that can be readily extended to other air pollutants, monitoring stations, and environmental forecasting applications.
